newsitem.title: USA: Mass. Senate takes up $700 mln convention center.
newsitem.headline: Mass. Senate takes up $700 mln convention center.

text.p: The Massachusetts Senate this week will take up the issue of a $700 million convention center for Boston and raises for some key members of the House Speaker's team.

Senate President Thomas Birmingham (D-Chelsea) said the Senate probably will adopt its version of the convention center legislation Thursday. Some significant changes are expected, though he would not give specifics.
"Overall, I think you'll see many more points of agreement than disagreement" between the House and Senate versions, is as far as Birmingham was willing to go.

In all, $717 million in state money would be spent under the House bill. It will be combined with $157 million from the city of Boston and pay for a $700 million, 600,000-square foot center near Fort Point Channel; a new $48.5 million civic center for Springfield and other projects.
Senators may have different ideas about new projects or different funding sources for the tourist facilities.
The House bill raises the hotel/motel tax to 12.45 percent from 9.7 percent in Boston, Cambridge, Worcester and Springfield.
Boston could raise the tax within city borders to 13.95 percent, with a vote of the city council.

In Boston, a new $10 surcharge would be levied on car rentals, and sightseeing tickets would be taxed $1 apiece. The money would help pay for civic center construction or improvement in Boston, Worcester and Springfield, and in all those cities a new $2 charge would be placed on parking at the centers.

Special revenue zones would be set up around the Boston convention center to capture the anticipated growth in sales and entertainment taxes and funnel them toward convention center construction. The city agreed to put up $157 million for the convention center in Boston, and pay half of any site acquisition costs above the high-end estimate of $205 million.

Senate leadership has been willing to pass a convention center bill for years, but the House speaker - first Charles Flaherty, now Thomas Finneran - has long been an obstacle. House leaders have argued any bill authorizing the borrowing for the center should also raise revenues to pay for most, if not all, the construction cost.

Last week, the House passed a convention center bill for the first time ever, but Finneran, in a controversial move, buried raises for a chose few House legislators in it and also moved to eliminate the special job protection enjoyed by Fracis Joyce, executive director of the Massachusetts Convention Center Authority.

The 1982 bill setting up the authority made no provision for Joyce's removal, guaranteeing his lifetime tenure. Birmingham's predecessor Senate President William Bulger made sure Joyce was protected when he drafted the legislation.

Now Joyce is expected to become a bargaining chip as Finneran tries to reward the selected committee chairmen with backpay raises and Birmingham tries to honor his predecessor and mentor's commitment.
